name: Simpson-Visser Black Bounce
description: Schwarzschild's metric with $\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$ written for the areal radius, which Alex Simpson and Matt Visser proposed in 2019. One length $a$ carries it from Schwarzschild's black hole through a regular black hole, whose inside bounces into another universe, and a one way wormhole to a traversable wormhole.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter $m$ is $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The recipe fits on one line: take Schwarzschild's metric and, wherever the radius $r$ stands as a number, write $\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$, leaving $dr$ as it is [simpson2019, bronnikov2022]. Its authors, Alex Simpson and Matt Visser, called it "carefully designed to be a minimalist modification of the ordinary Schwarzschild spacetime" when they posted it in December 2018 [simpson2019]. The sphere $r = 0$, where Schwarzschild has his singularity, now has the area $4\pi a^2$, and $r$ runs on through it to negative values [simpson2019]. They offered it as a new candidate in a line that James Bardeen began in 1968, the regular black holes, which keep a horizon and do away with the singularity [simpson2019].¶What the metric describes depends on how $a$ compares with the Schwarzschild radius $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$ [simpson2019]. For $a < r_s$ there are two horizons, at $r = \pm\sqrt{r_s^2 - a^2}$, and whatever falls through the first crosses the sphere $r = 0$, now a spacelike surface on which the areal radius stops shrinking at $a$ and starts to grow, and leaves through the second into another asymptotically flat universe [simpson2019]. Simpson and Visser named this a "black-bounce", a bounce "into a future incarnation of the universe" [simpson2019]. At $a = r_s$ the horizons merge on the sphere of least area, an extremal null throat that can be crossed in one direction only, and for $a > r_s$ no horizon is left: the metric is a wormhole in the sense of Michael Morris and Kip Thorne, open both ways [simpson2019, morris1988]. With the mass set to zero it is the wormhole that Homer Ellis and Kirill Bronnikov found in 1973 [tsukamoto2021, ellis1973, bronnikov1973].¶Their conformal diagram for $a < r_s$ is to be set beside Kruskal and Szekeres's for Schwarzschild's black hole: "the major difference is that the singularity has been replaced by a spacelike hypersurface representing a 'bounce'" [simpson2019]. Each bounce leads into a new copy of the exterior with a black hole of its own, so the diagram climbs "ad infinitum" [simpson2019]. Every component of the curvature is finite for $a > 0$, and the Kretschmann scalar on the sphere of least area is $(9r_s^2 - 16ar_s + 12a^2)/a^6$ [simpson2019]. Read through Einstein's equations, the metric needs matter that violates the null energy condition everywhere off the horizons [simpson2019]. The black hole is colder than Schwarzschild's, its surface gravity smaller by the factor $\sqrt{1 - a^2/r_s^2}$, which vanishes at $a = r_s$ [simpson2019]. Circular orbits stay where Schwarzschild has them: light circles at the areal radius $3r_s/2$, and the innermost stable orbit is at $3r_s$ [simpson2019].¶The metric was not derived from any field equations, and in 2020 Bronnikov and Roman Konoplya said so plainly: it "is not a solution of any field equations and was simply designed ad hoc" [bronnikovkonoplya2020]. Black holes with a bounce inside had come out of field equations before: Bronnikov and Julio Fabris found them in 2006 for a phantom scalar field, a field whose kinetic energy is negative, with an expanding universe of de Sitter kind beyond the bounce [bronnikov2006, bronnikov2022]. Two years after that remark, Bronnikov and Rahul Kumar Walia supplied the fields for Simpson and Visser's metric itself: a phantom scalar with a potential, together with a magnetic field obeying a nonlinear electrodynamics [bronnikov2022]. Neither field can do it alone [bronnikov2022]. The result, they wrote, "uplifts the status of SV-like space-times from ad-hoc mathematical models to a class of exact solution of gravitational field equations" [bronnikov2022].¶Let the mass depend on the null time, as Prahlad Vaidya had for Schwarzschild's metric, and the geometry can change its kind: a black bounce grows, a wormhole accretes null dust until a horizon forms around its throat, a black bounce evaporates and leaves a wormhole behind [simpson2019vaidya]. Simpson, Prado Martín-Moruno, and Visser worked those cases out in February 2019, with the metric rewritten in Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates [simpson2019vaidya]. Set spinning by the Newman-Janis procedure, the metric becomes a family that is Kerr's when the new length vanishes, and otherwise a rotating wormhole or a rotating regular black hole with one or two horizons [mazza2021]. Jacopo Mazza, Edgardo Franzin, and Stefano Liberati built it in 2021, and with Simpson and Visser made the same substitution in the Reissner-Nordström and Kerr-Newman metrics that year [mazza2021, franzin2021]. Francisco Lobo, Manuel Rodrigues, Marcos Silva, Simpson, and Visser built further black bounces from other mass functions, with two or more horizons [lobo2021].¶How would an observer tell a black bounce from a black hole? By its ringing, once $a$ has passed $r_s$: M. S. Churilova and Zdeněk Stuchlík computed the quasinormal modes of all three kinds and found echoes following the black hole's ringdown on the wormhole side of the transition [churilova2020]. Naoki Tsukamoto worked out the bending of light for every $a$ and $r_s$, with the areal radius $\rho = \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$ as a second radial coordinate, and found that at $a = 3r_s/2$ the two photon spheres and the antiphoton sphere at the throat merge into one marginally unstable orbit, where the deflection angle no longer diverges logarithmically [tsukamoto2021].¶The shadow does not help: Haroldo Lima Junior, Luís Crispino, Pedro Cunha, and Carlos Herdeiro pointed out that the hypersurfaces of constant areal radius are isometric to Schwarzschild's, so the black hole casts a shadow of Schwarzschild's size whatever $a$ is [lima2021]. Sunny Vagnozzi and fourteen collaborators found the Event Horizon Telescope's image of Sagittarius A* consistent with the black hole, the black bounce, and both wormholes, for every $a$ below $3r_s/2$, which made the metric "the first example (among those we have considered) of a BH mimicker space-time which could be a viable candidate in light of Sgr A$^*$'s shadow" [vagnozzi2023]. Fitting the rotating metric to the X-ray reflection spectrum of the black hole binary EXO 1846-031, Shafqat Riaz and seven collaborators bounded the new length at $0.49\,GM/c^2$ with 90% confidence [riaz2022]. The gravitational waves of GW190707A gave them $0.72\,GM/c^2$ [riaz2022].

related.text: Set $a = 0$ and the bounce closes up into Schwarzschild's singularity. Simpson and Visser wrote $\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$ for his $r$ and left everything else alone [simpson2019].
With the mass switched off, $r_s = 0$, the metric is Ellis and Bronnikov's wormhole, and $a$ is the radius $\ell$ of its throat [tsukamoto2021, ellis1973, bronnikov1973].

The general static wormhole a traveller could cross. For $a > r_s$ the black bounce is the one with $e^{2\Phi} = 1 - r_s/\rho$ and $b = r_s + a^2/\rho - r_sa^2/\rho^2$, in the areal radius $\rho$ [morris1988, tsukamoto2021].
Between the horizons $r$ is a time, and the inside of the black bounce is a Kantowski-Sachs cosmology whose spheres shrink to the radius $a$ and grow again [bronnikov2022].

The black bounce has Reissner and Nordström's tower of universes, two horizons to each black hole, with another asymptotically flat region where their timelike singularity stands. At $a = r_s$ it looks from outside much as their extremal black hole does [simpson2019, bronnikov2022].

The other way to turn Schwarzschild's black hole into a wormhole with one number. Damour and Solodukhin changed $g_{tt}$ and kept the horizon's sphere as the throat, where Simpson and Visser changed the radius [damour2007, simpson2019].

Let the mass depend on the null time, as Vaidya did for Schwarzschild's metric, and a wormhole can accrete its way into a black bounce, or a black bounce evaporate into a wormhole [simpson2019vaidya].
The black bounce set spinning by the Newman-Janis procedure is Kerr's metric when the new length vanishes [mazza2021].

The regular black hole of 1968. Bardeen's closes over a regular centre with de Sitter space at its core, where the black bounce opens through a throat into another universe [ansoldi2008, simpson2019].

A regular black hole with a centre and a core of de Sitter space. Simpson and Visser counted Hayward's among the traditional regular black holes, which close over a regular centre where theirs opens through a throat [simpson2019, hayward2006].
A universe filled with phantom energy, the kind of scalar field that holds up this bounce, which pulls the universe apart at a finite time [caldwell2002, caldwell2003].
A bounce of a whole universe, which loop quantum cosmology puts where the big bang was [ashtekar2006bounce].

coordinates.name: Simpson-Visser
domains: r = \pm\sqrt{r_s^2 - a^2} \;\text{(the horizons, where } a < r_s\text{)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$
Length that sets the least areal radius, $a \ge 0$; at $a = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's
Areal radius of the sphere at $r$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ running over the whole real line, and we write $\rho = \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$ for the areal radius of the sphere at $r$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.

coordinates.name: Areal Radius

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the mass parameter, $r_s = 2Gm/c^2$
Length that sets the least areal radius, $a \ge 0$; at $a = 0$ the metric is Schwarzschild's

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$ on either side of the sphere of least area, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ the areal radius, so $r = \pm\sqrt{\rho^2 - a^2}$ in Simpson and Visser's chart. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter $s$, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/ds$.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} + \dfrac{r_s\left(\rho - r_s\right)\left(\rho^2 - a^2\right)}{2\rho^5}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r_s\,\rho^2 + 2a^2\,\rho - 3r_s\,a^2}{2\rho\left(\rho - r_s\right)\left(\rho^2 - a^2\right)}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\left(\rho - r_s\right)\left(\rho^2 - a^2\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\left(\rho - r_s\right)\left(\rho^2 - a^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{\rho^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s/\sqrt{r^2 + a^2}\right)^{-1}$, and we write $\rho = \sqrt{r^2 + a^2}$ for the areal radius of the sphere at $r$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
